title: Burrata vs Mozzarella: Same Family, Very Different Center

seo.title: Burrata vs Mozzarella: Texture, Flavor, and Best Uses
seo.meta_description: Mozzarella is a stretched-curd cheese with a consistent interior. Burrata is a pouch of mozzarella-like curd filled with stracciatella and cream, making it richer, softer, and more perishable.
seo.search_intent: Explain how burrata differs from fresh mozzarella in structure, richness, storage, cooking behavior, and serving.

excerpt: Burrata and fresh mozzarella share a stretched-curd heritage, but burrata is built around a creamy filling. Mozzarella is uniform all the way through; burrata has an outer shell surrounding stracciatella and cream, so it is softer, richer, and best eaten very fresh.
content_html:
Burrata is often described as “creamier mozzarella,” but the construction explains the difference more precisely. Fresh mozzarella is a stretched-curd cheese whose texture is broadly consistent from surface to center. Burrata uses a mozzarella-like outer pouch to hold a filling of stracciatella—shreds or strands of curd—mixed with cream. Cut a burrata and the center flows; cut a ball of mozzarella and it stays cohesive. That structural difference affects richness, handling, cooking, and how each cheese is best served.

Both begin with pasta filata technique

Mozzarella belongs to the pasta filata, or stretched-curd, family. Acidified curd is heated and worked until the proteins align enough to stretch, creating the elastic, milky texture associated with fresh mozzarella. Burrata makers use a similar stretched curd to form the outer shell, then fill it before sealing. Because the two cheeses share that foundation, their outside flavor can be similar. The dramatic contrast comes from the center, where cream raises richness and moisture and stracciatella adds tender strands.

Burrata is richer and less uniform

Fresh mozzarella varies in fat depending on the milk and product, but it is usually a relatively moist cheese with a clean dairy flavor. Burrata’s cream filling generally increases fat and calorie density in the part you spoon from the center. There is no single universal nutrition number because ball size, milk type, cream ratio, and serving size differ. If nutrition matters, compare labels by weight. The important culinary expectation is simpler: burrata is lush and spoonable, while mozzarella is springier and easier to slice or tear neatly.

Their best uses are not identical

Mozzarella is versatile. It works in caprese salad, sandwiches, pasta, and many cooked dishes, and low-moisture mozzarella is specifically suited to pizza because it releases less water. Burrata shines when its creamy center can remain visible and fluid: tomatoes, roasted vegetables, grilled bread, peaches, prosciutto, olive oil, or a warm plate of pasta added just before serving. Baking burrata for a long time sacrifices much of what makes it distinctive. If you want dramatic creaminess at the table, burrata is the better choice; if you need slicing, stretching, or controlled melt, mozzarella is easier.

Freshness and refrigeration matter

Both are high-moisture cheeses that require refrigeration, and burrata is especially associated with a short quality window after production. Follow the package date and storage instructions, keep the cheese cold, and avoid leaving it at room temperature for extended periods. Once opened, use clean utensils and consume promptly. People at higher risk from foodborne illness should also check that fresh soft cheeses are made with pasteurized milk; FDA advises consumers to choose pasteurized products for safer handling.

Can mozzarella replace burrata?

Yes when the dish needs mild fresh cheese rather than a flowing center. Fresh mozzarella with a spoonful of ricotta or cream will not reproduce burrata exactly, but it can give a similar mild dairy contrast. The reverse substitution is less useful in recipes that depend on mozzarella’s elasticity or relatively predictable moisture. Burrata can make a pizza or baked dish wet and rich because the filling releases cream. For cooking, treat burrata as a finishing cheese more often than a structural cheese.

Choose by texture first

If the choice is between two good fresh products, there is no need to rank one as universally superior. Choose mozzarella for bounce, clean slices, and versatile cooking; choose burrata for a fragile pouch and creamy, spoonable center. Serve either near room temperature for flavor only after keeping it safely refrigerated until shortly before the meal. A little salt, olive oil, and acidic or fresh produce usually complement both without overwhelming their mild milk flavor.

Temperature at serving also affects perception. Straight from the refrigerator, both cheeses taste firmer and less aromatic. Letting a portion sit briefly before serving can reveal more flavor and soften the texture, but do not leave high-moisture fresh cheese unrefrigerated for extended periods. For a platter, bring out only what you expect to eat and return the rest to the refrigerator. This preserves both the creamy experience and safer handling.

faq.question: Is burrata just mozzarella with cream?
faq.answer: Burrata has a mozzarella-like stretched-curd shell, but the center is filled with stracciatella and cream, so its structure is different.

faq.question: Which is better for pizza?
faq.answer: Mozzarella is usually more practical, especially low-moisture mozzarella. Burrata is often better added after baking as a creamy finishing cheese.

faq.question: Which has more fat?
faq.answer: Burrata is generally richer because of the cream filling, but exact nutrition depends on the specific product and serving size.
